items.page_hint: Ch 17 §4, bullet 'The 25 ms/token in W is the TPOT budget, not a measured per-step time'; also Ch 15 §3 'Compute demand versus peak' and Ch 17 §4 'Simultaneous feasibility check'
items.issue: The 5.2 ms/step floor counts only weight traffic. It omits the per-step KV read traffic, which at the canonical geometry is the larger term: every decode step must read the full KV of every resident sequence (24.9037 GB per 9,500-token request), so at the canonical occupancy of 17 resident requests a step reads 140 GB (weights) + 17 × 24.9037 GB (KV) ≈ 563.4 GB, i.e. ≈21.0 ms/step at 26.8 TB/s — about 4x the printed floor. The inference 'a well-tuned decode can run well under the 25 ms SLO' therefore does not follow at the canonical context length and concurrency. The same omission makes the decode leg's feasibility at the canonical peak invisible: 12,000 output tok/s x (140/B + 24.1) GB/token ≈ 388 TB/s at B = 17, roughly 14x the host's HBM bandwidth.
items.quoted_clause: The decode-bandwidth floor for the canonical 8×H100 host is 140 GB ÷ (8 × 3.35 TB/s) ≈ 5.2 ms/step, so a well-tuned decode can run well under the 25 ms SLO.
items.fix_instruction: Add the KV term: bytes/step = 140 GB + B × 24.9 GB; step time = that ÷ 26.8 TB/s; at B = 17 → ~21 ms/step. Re-anchor Ch 17's sensitivity band (5.2/10/25) on the corrected floor, add a decode-leg feasibility check at the canonical peak load, and rewrite 'well under the 25 ms SLO'.
items.evidence: chapter-17.md (exact): 'The decode‑bandwidth floor for the canonical 8×H100 host is 140 GB ÷ (8 × 3.35 TB/s) ≈ 5.2 ms/step, so a well‑tuned decode can run well under the 25 ms SLO.' Arithmetic: 140/26.8 = 5.22 ✓ — weights only. Per-request KV verified: chapter-17.md 'Each request at 9,200 input + 300 output reserves a **9,500‑token max** KV of 9,500 ×2.62 MB ≈ 24.9 GB... C = 436 GB ÷ 24.9037 GB ≈ **17.5 concurrent requests**... floor **17**' ✓. Recompute: 17 × 24.9037 = 423.36 + 140 = 563.36 GB/step ÷ 26,800 GB/s = 21.02 ms/step ≈ 4× the printed floor ✓; and 12,000 output tok/s (40 × 300) × (140/17 + 24.1 GB/tok) = 388,000 GB/s = 388 TB/s ÷ 26.8 ≈ 14.5× HBM bandwidth ✓. 'never quantified' verified: grep across chapter-02/06/08/15/17/20 for (B × KV, batch × KV, weights + B, 140 + B) — zero matches; chapter-15.md §1 names the cost only qualitatively: 'the memory traffic of KV cache reads and writes on every token step'. At 21 ms/step (ideal) vs the 25 ms budget there is no 'well under' (84% of budget — any inefficiency exceeds it).

items.page_hint: Ch 17 §4 (W_GPU-exec row of the time-symbol table; 'The 25 ms/token in W is the TPOT budget'); Ch 15 §1 (canonical SLO sentence)
items.issue: Ch 15 §1 states the canonical SLO as 'TTFT median <= 1.2 s, p95 <= 2 s, TPOT <= 40 ms (Ch 4/Ch 14)'. Ch 17 derives the canonical service time from a 25 ms/token budget and calls it 'the least-favourable (budget) pole'. 25 ms is more favourable than the book's own 40 ms SLO, so the 'conservative' claim is false against the stated SLO, and the sensitivity band (5.2 / 10 / 25 ms) omits the SLO pole entirely. The sensitivity band... at 5.2 ms/step W ≈ 2.6 s...; at 10 ms/step W ≈ 4.1 s...; at the 25 ms budget W ≈ 8.6 s (in‑flight ≈ 344, ~21 hosts)' — band 5.2/10/25 with no SLO pole ✓. chapter-15.md §1: 'The canonical SLO this chapter measures against: TTFT median ≤ 1.2 s, p95 ≤ 2 s, TPOT ≤ 40 ms (Ch 4/Ch 14)' ✓ exists — while Ch 4 says 'TPOT budget ~25 ms/token; p95 TPOT ≤ 35 ms' and Ch 14 says 'TPOT ~25 ms/token' and 'median TPOT about 25 ms' (grep) — the 40 ms matches neither of the chapters it cites. items.figure: FIGURE 15.1 — FlashAttention: the same math, far less HBM traffic
items.issue: The BEFORE panel is annotated "O(L²) HBM traffic" while the AFTER panel carries no complexity label, which invites the false inference that FlashAttention is asymptotically cheaper in HBM traffic. It is not: with d fixed, naive attention is Θ(L²) HBM element-accesses and FlashAttention is Θ(L²d²/M) — the same order, with a constant-factor reduction set by on-chip SRAM capacity M. The caption's scope note ("the gain is fewer HBM round-trips, not a change to the attention mathematics") addresses the mathematics, not the asymptotics, so the misconception survives the caption. This is exactly the inference a reader is likely to carry into later capacity arithmetic.
items.fix_instruction: Add a complexity qualifier to the AFTER annotation or caption, e.g. 'still Θ(L²) HBM accesses — the gain is a constant factor set by on-chip capacity (d²/M), not a lower order'.
items.evidence: p257 verified: 'O(L²)' appears only in the BEFORE red annotation; the AFTER green annotation ('KV reused per tile — no single global K/V pass; no L×L intermediate at HBM') carries no complexity term, and the caption's scope note (chapter-15.md:36) addresses the mathematics only — with d fixed both paths are Θ(L²) HBM element accesses, so the one-sided label invites an asymptotic reading.

items.issue: The in-plot formula 'f(r)=(S+P/r)/(S+P)  P=40%, S=60%' uses symbols S and P that are never defined in the figure, caption, or adjacent prose. The drawn curve is consistent only if P is the reusable prefix share (f(10)=(0.6+0.04)/1.0=0.64, matching the plotted ~64; asymptote 60%=S). A competent reader who reads S as 'shared' (the natural reading) computes f(10)=(0.06+0.40)/1.0=0.46 and finds the formula contradicts the plotted curve — a plausible-but-wrong inference permitted by the figure.
items.fix_instruction: Extend the in-plot note to 'f(r)=(S+P/r)/(S+P); P=40% prefix (reusable), S=60% suffix' or add the same definition to the caption; re-render and confirm a reader can state what P and S mean from the figure alone.
items.evidence: Page 259 image shows green in-plot note 'f(r)=(S+P/r)/(S+P) / P=40%, S=60%'; caption (chapter-15.md line 48) defines only r; grep design/manuscript for 'f(r)|P = 40|S = 60' returned 0 matches, so S and P are undefined in figure, caption and prose (only render/fig_ch15_goodput.py line 34 comment defines them: P=reusable prefix, S=unique suffix).

items.figure: FIGURE 15.2 — Prefill caching vs batching: two independent effects
items.issue: The smallest text in the figure appears to fall below the 8 pt floor for figure in-text annotations, and it is carrying the most decision-relevant content. The panel (b) red callout ("diminishing gains past ~6 (...); goodput still rises; tail latency keeps rising") is the only place the reader is told that the illustrative curve does not reach a hard plateau and that tail latency keeps degrading — the caveat the caption also carries. The panel (a) formula note ("f(r)=5/(1+r); P=40%, S=60%") is likewise small. At print size these are the first things a reader will skip, and they are the things that must not be skipped.
